note: The canonical department roster. new_plan.py writes one section per department into plan/departments.md and check_plan.py checks every one is present and complete, or marked not applicable with a reason. Tool names are deliberately absent: they go stale, so each plan chooses concrete tools with verified prices at the time it is written.

departments.name: Product
departments.lens: Builds for the job the customer is hiring the product to do, not for the feature list. Sees the roadmap as a sequence of bets, each with a way to know if it paid off.
asks: How do we hear from customers every week, not only when something breaks?
What is the one metric that tells us the core loop works, and who looks at it when?
How do we decide what not to build, and who can overrule it?
Where does feedback from support, sales and reviews land, and who reads it?

departments.name: Engineering
departments.lens: Thinks about the second year of the codebase on the first day: environments, release safety, review, and how the team will change things without fear.
asks: How does a change get from a laptop to production, and how is it undone?
What runs in CI, and what blocks a merge?
Who gets paged when production breaks, and what do they see first?
What is the budget for tech debt, and how is it spent rather than promised?

departments.name: Design and brand
departments.lens: Consistency comes from one source of truth that every surface reads, not from taste. Owns everything a user sees, including link previews, emails and store screenshots.
asks: Where do the design tokens live, and what stops a surface from hardcoding a value?
Who signs off on a screen, and against what checklist?
Which assets are generated, and which would rot if made by hand?
How is accessibility checked before release, not after a complaint?

departments.name: Data and analytics
departments.lens: A number nobody trusts is worse than no number. Owns the event contract, the warehouse and the handful of metrics the company runs on.
asks: Where does raw event data land, and can we query it ourselves in a year?
Which events are authoritative from the server and which from clients?
Who defines a metric, and where is the definition written?
How do we run an experiment and know the answer is real?

departments.name: Security and privacy engineering
departments.lens: Assumes the breach and plans the blast radius. Knows that the first enterprise customer will send a security questionnaire, and that the answers have to be true.
asks: What is the threat model: who would attack this, and what would they want?
Who has access to production data, and how is that logged and reviewed?
What happens in the first hour of an incident, and who decides to notify users?
When will a customer first ask for a security certification, and what does reaching it require?

departments.name: Marketing and content
departments.lens: Positioning before promotion. Knows which channel the business will live or die by, and builds the machine that feeds it rather than doing one-off pushes.
asks: What do we say in one sentence, to whom, and how is it different from the alternative?
Which channel carries the first thousand customers, and what does it cost per customer?
What content do we produce every week, and who or what produces it?
How do we know which campaign produced which customer?

departments.name: Sales and partnerships
departments.lens: Revenue is a pipeline with stages and conversion rates, not a hope. Knows that the first ten deals are founder-led and that the process must be written before the first hire.
asks: Who exactly is the ideal customer, and how do we find a hundred of them by name?
What are the stages from first contact to signed, and what moves a deal between them?
Who can discount, by how much, and what does the contract look like?
Which partners or integrations would bring customers we cannot reach alone?

departments.name: Customer success and support
departments.lens: Retention is decided in the first week of use. Knows the twenty questions every new customer will ask and answers them before they are asked.
asks: What does a new customer have to do in their first week to stay, and how do we make sure they do it?
Where do customers ask for help, how fast do we answer, and who answers at 2am?
What can a customer fix themselves, and what needs us?
How does what support hears reach product, every week?

departments.name: Trust and safety
departments.lens: Every feature that connects people is also a way for one of them to hurt another. Plans the abuse before the abuser finds it.
asks: How could someone use this product to harm another person, and what stops them?
How does a user report something, and how fast does a human see it?
What do we do about fraud, fake accounts and scams, before and after the fact?
What happens when law enforcement or a lawyer asks for data?

departments.name: Operations
departments.lens: Owns everything that has to happen for the product to work that is not code: supply, vendors, fulfilment, and the runbooks for the day something fails.
asks: What manual work happens every week to keep this running, and what breaks when volume doubles?
Which vendors do we depend on, and what is the plan if one disappears?
For a marketplace: how do we recruit, vet and keep the supply side?
Where are the runbooks, and has anyone actually followed one?

departments.name: Finance and accounting
departments.lens: Cash is the only number that can end the company this month. Keeps the books clean enough that taxes, fundraising or a sale never stall on them.
asks: Who keeps the books, monthly, and when do they close?
Which taxes do we file, where, and when — including sales tax on what we sell?
How many months of cash do we have, and who checks it every month?
Is the cap table, entity and banking set up so we could raise or sell without cleanup?

departments.name: Legal and compliance
departments.lens: Cheapest at the design stage, most expensive after launch. Owns the register, the terms, the privacy program, IP and the contracts.
asks: Which rules apply because of what we do, where we are, and who our users are?
Do our terms and privacy notice match what the product actually does?
Do we own our code, name, brand and content — including what contractors made?
Which decisions need a lawyer before launch, and what does that review cost?

departments.name: People and hiring
departments.lens: The first five hires set the culture by default. Plans who is needed when, at what cost, and what the founder stops doing as each one joins.
asks: What will the founder stop doing first, and who takes it over?
At what customer count or revenue does each hire become necessary?
Contractor or employee — and what does the law say about the difference here?
How does a new person learn how things are done here without asking the founder?

departments.name: Leadership and strategy
departments.lens: Decides what the company will not do. Owns the cadence that turns numbers into decisions, and the record of why each decision was made.
asks: Which three numbers do we review every week, and what do we do when one moves?
Where is the record of decisions and their reasons?
What would make us change strategy, and how would we notice in time?
How does the founder spend their week, and is that the highest-value use of it?

departments.name: International and localization
departments.lens: Each new country is a new product: language, currency, payment rails, tax, law and culture. Decides what has to be true in the code before the first one, so the second is cheap.
asks: Which country is next, and what is the trigger to enter it?
Are strings, currencies, dates and addresses ready for more than one locale today?
Which payment rails, tax registrations and local entities does each country need?
Who checks that the product makes sense in that culture, not just that language?

departments.name: AI and automation
departments.lens: Treats models as a dependency with a cost, a failure rate and a supplier. Decides which work in every other department an agent can run, and how its output is checked.
asks: Which product features use a model, what does each call cost, and what happens when it is wrong?
How do we test model output before shipping a change, and track quality after?
Which recurring work across departments can an agent do today, with what human check?
What user data reaches a model provider, and does the privacy notice say so?
